title: Man found not guilty of sex offences on Camber Sands beach
text:
A man from Kent has been found not guilty of a number of sexual offences against a woman on Camber Sands.

Mohammed Maatoug, 34, of Boxley Road, Maidstone, was arrested in August 2025 after a woman in her 50s reported being attacked while sunbathing in the dunes on 25 August 2025.

He was found not guilty of two counts of sexual assault and one count of assault by penetration. The trial concluded at Lewes Crown Court on Friday, the BBC reported.

title: New management takes over 15th century Red Lion pub in Hooe
text:
The Red Lion, a 15th century pub in Denbigh Road, Hooe, near Battle, has been taken over by new management.

The pub announced the handover in a social media statement, saying it is open every lunchtime and dinner, Tuesday through Saturday.

According to tourism guide Experience Sussex, the building was originally constructed in 1495 and converted into a pub in the 1600s. It was once a haunt for smugglers and customs officers, and its attic housed a secret tobacco mill that is reputed to have inspired the saying "money for old rope", The Argus reported.

Customers said the reopening got off to a good start, with one guest praising the roast dinner on the pub's first day and another booking a return lunch after visiting on Saturday.

title: Hastings Castle to get £288,500 from Historic England for repairs
text:
Hastings Borough Council has been awarded £288,500 from Historic England's Heritage at Risk Capital Fund for repairs to Hastings Castle.

The grant, combined with £200,000 from the council, will pay for urgent conservation work, including stabilising vulnerable sections of the curtain walls, conserving the tower wall, chapel arch and Collegiate Church remains, repairing the Ladies' Parlour wall, and addressing vegetation, masonry defects and other vulnerable historic features.

Cllr Julia Hilton, the council's deputy leader and lead councillor for shaping place, regeneration and community wealth building, said the castle was a key part of the town's and the country's heritage, and that the work was needed to protect both the scheduled monument and the public visiting the site.

Louise Brennan, director of regions at Historic England, said the funding would support urgent conservation needs while helping projects move towards sustainable futures.

title: Hastings Philharmonic Choir to sing Schubert and Saint-Saëns
text:
The Hastings Philharmonic Choir's next concert, Songs of Light, brings two choral masterpieces to All Saints Church in the Old Town on Saturday 7 November.

The programme is built around Schubert's Mass in G and Saint-Saëns' Oratorio de Noël, the Christmas Oratorio. The choir will be joined by soloists including Beth Yates and Helen May (sopranos), Kerry Gentleman (contralto), John Twitchen (tenor) and Geoff Williams (baritone), with the strings of the Hastings Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Marcio da Silva.

Both composers were young when they wrote the works. Schubert, aged 18, composed the Mass in G in six days in March 1815, and Saint-Saëns, 23, finished his oratorio in under two weeks before its first performance in Paris in December 1858.

Tickets range from free to £22.50 and are on sale via the choir's website, The Bookkeeper on Kings Road, St Leonards, and Bookbuster on Queens Road, Hastings.

title: Gruffalo parade to close Hastings Storytelling Festival on the Stade
text:
The Hastings Storytelling Festival comes to a close on Sunday, October 25, with a free Children's Day on the Stade and a Gruffalo themed parade through the Old Town.

Produced by 18 Hours in partnership with the Hastings Storytelling Festival charity, this year's festival, themed Connections, has been running in venues across the town over recent days.

On Sunday, the Stade hosts puppetry, music, walkabout acts and creative workshops, including Pirate Gem's Swashbuckling Adventure show from CBeebies, Long Nose Puppets, Circo Rum Baba's Pesky Pirates and Mermaid Tales on giant seahorses.

Festival patron Axel Scheffler, the illustrator of The Gruffalo, has invited guest author and illustrator Tor Freeman to join the celebrations. A spokesperson for 18 Hours said everyone is welcome to dress up and join the parade, lining up from 2.45pm to parade with local drumming groups and hand painted costumes created by carnival artist Donna Fox.

title: Fears of hungry children over half-term after holiday food vouchers axed
text:
Families across East Sussex have not received automatic food vouchers for the October half term after the county council ended the school holiday scheme, raising fears that vulnerable children could go hungry.

The vouchers, which supported households whose children receive benefits-related free school meals, were stopped by East Sussex County Council after the May half term, following changes to government funding. The previous Household Support Fund was replaced by the Crisis and Resilience Fund, which is intended for households facing immediate hardship rather than blanket holiday vouchers.

Barry Ashley, who runs The Grumpy Cook cafe in Hastings, said he understood the new fund was managed by Citizens Advice 1066 and was aimed at sudden financial shocks, which school holidays do not fall into. His cafe will offer free meals to children during the half term, with no adult purchase required, as it did over the summer.

Penny Downes of Rye Foodbank said in July that she was very concerned about the end of the scheme, and the Food Foundation's latest figures show 39.2 per cent of children in the Hastings and Rye constituency are living in poverty. Liberal Democrat opposition leader Cllr Kathryn Field said she was concerned the most isolated families might not access the support and that children risked going hungry.

A council spokesman said support is available for any family in East Sussex that needs it, and that the way it is delivered has changed in line with government funding changes. The council said it would spend £7.3 million over the next year through the Crisis and Resilience Fund, on services including debt advice, community food schemes, holiday clubs with meals and help with household essentials.

title: On this day 1823: New town hall market opens in the High Street
text:
On 25 October 1823, the new town hall in the High Street opened its ground floor to the market traders, with 14 stalls taking up their positions.

The foundation stone of the building had been laid just over four months earlier, on 2 June 1823. The market floor offered meat on Wednesdays and Saturdays, and fruit, fish, eggs and the like on other days, with the market closed on Sundays.

As the town's needs changed, the ground floor took on other roles, becoming home to a police station and a fire station. The building is now the Old Town Hall Museum.

title: Bexhill empty shops plan opens for public consultation
text:
Rother District Council has asked residents and businesses to have their say on a plan to tackle long-term empty shops in Bexhill.

The council is consulting on a proposal to designate Bexhill town centre as an area where High Street Rental Auction powers could be used. The powers, introduced by government, are designed to help bring persistently vacant commercial properties back into use and support high street regeneration.

A recent audit of commercial premises in the town centre found 55 vacant units out of 439 properties surveyed, a vacancy rate of 12.5 per cent. The council said the figure is slightly below the national average, but the audit identified clusters of empty premises along London Road, Sackville Road, Sea Road and Devonshire Road. Bexhill is being considered as a pilot location for any future use of the scheme within the district.

Councillor Christine Bayliss, cabinet member for regeneration, said the council wanted to hear directly from residents, businesses, landlords and community partners before any further decisions were made. The council said Bexhill still benefits from a strong mix of independent businesses and hospitality venues, but the audit highlighted concerns around long-term vacant units and ageing buildings.

title: Buses replace trains between Tonbridge and Wadhurst from Saturday
text:
No trains will run between Tonbridge and Wadhurst from Saturday 24 October until Sunday 1 November, as Network Rail carries out major work on the Hastings line. Rail replacement buses will operate throughout, and the closure extends to Battle on the final day.

Engineers will use the closure to renew worn slab track in Grove Hill Tunnel, just south of Tunbridge Wells, and to remove three temporary speed restrictions: two between Crowhurst and Battle and one between Etchingham and Robertsbridge. The restrictions were put in place after the record hot and dry summer left soil beneath the track drying out and shrinking.

Buses will also replace trains between Wadhurst and Hastings from 10.30pm on Saturday 31 October until 7am on Sunday 1 November. Scott Brightwell, director of safety and performance at Southeastern, said the work is an investment in the Hastings line and asked passengers to plan ahead and allow extra time for their journeys. Tickets from Hastings and Ore will be accepted through to Ashford International and onto London St Pancras highspeed services.

title: New Orleans duo Odom-Kunkel to play the Jenny Lind in November
text:
Desert rock voices from New Orleans are making a detour to the Hastings music scene. Bassist-vocalist Stoo Odom and Roger Kunkel, both members of the Californian desert rock band Thin White Rope, will play the Jenny Lind on Friday 20 November, according to the Hastings Online Times.

The pair, reunited as Odom-Kunkel, are touring the UK to release their new EP 'Sniffing Spirits', which marries desert noir guitar with recitation, low-toned bass and improvisation. They will share the stage with Stray Bentos, the Hastings-based evolving collective fronted by Jude Montague and Danny Brittain, on the venue's Latin-themed Friday evenings.

Asked why he has picked Hastings for the tour, Stoo said: "Y'all are real sweet. And it's a tiny version of my beloved San Francisco, but with foxes, slow worms, and jellied eels." The gig starts at 8pm and is free.

title: Hastings and Rye MP criticises Bayeux Tapestry ticket phone system
places: Hastings, St Leonards, Rye, Bexhill, Battle
text:
The MP for Hastings and Rye has criticised the phone line the British Museum set up for local residents to book tickets for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition.

The museum offered people from '1066 Country', the towns with the historic link to the 1066 battle, an early chance to book the latest tranche of tickets from Monday this week, provided they could prove they lived in the area.

But Helena Dollimore, the MP for Hastings and Rye, said constituents were being kept on hold for hours. One person booked after two hours and 38 minutes in the queue, she said, and another was on hold for two and a half hours. She called the system 'glitchy and shambolic' and asked why constituents had to work on a phone line when online booking was clearly possible for others.

A British Museum spokesperson said demand for the exhibition had been 'exceptionally high' and that the offer to residents was on a first-come, first-served basis. All residents remain able to book tickets as part of the general sale on 21 October, and a third tranche of tickets is due to be released in the new year.

title: West Hill Lift gets £531,000 from National Lottery Heritage Fund
text:
The National Lottery Heritage Fund has offered £531,000 in development funding to Hastings Borough Council to secure the long-term future of the West Hill Lift, the Grade II listed lift that runs up the cliff from George Street to Hastings Castle.

The money will pay for the detailed design work and planning consents the council says it needs before making a further bid for funding to fully restore the lift, which requires major work to improve accessibility and reliability.

A council spokesperson indicated the full restoration is likely to cost around £3.8 million, 'but it very much depends on what the development stage shows'.

Cllr Julia Hilton, deputy leader of the council and lead councillor for regeneration, said the future of the lift is 'a vital part' of the Hastings Castle project funded by the Town Deal, and thanked the Heritage Fund and National Lottery players for the grant.

title: Warm Homes Plan cuts would be 'terrible blunder', local energy service warns
text:
A local energy advice service has warned that cuts to the government's Warm Homes Plan would be a 'terrible blunder' for households across East Sussex.

The Hastings Online Times reports the government is set to slash funding for the plan in next week's budget, following a Guardian report that ministers were 'preparing to slash the amount of money available', including hundreds of millions of pounds from the Boiler Upgrade Scheme, which helps households switch from gas boilers to cleaner heating such as heat pumps.

Energise Sussex Coast, which runs a free energy advice service across the county, says the cut would hurt households, the climate and national security. Its director, Kate Meakin, said that in the midst of the current gas crisis it was worse for the government to cut funding for a plan that would reduce Britain's exposure to fossil fuel markets.

The move has also been criticised by the innovation charity Nesta, which said it would 'take the wind out of an industry at a critical stage of development'.

title: Hastings artist to launch book of paintings made through cancer
text:
Hastings artist Helen Slater will launch her book Uninvited on the afternoon of Sunday 25 October, hosted by The Peripheral Space Project.

Ms Slater, who works in acrylic, began painting on 31 July, the day she was told she had breast cancer. Colour, texture and abstract form became a way to express what she described as a cascade of words no one expected to hear: tumour, scans, hormone blockers, operation.

She kept creating throughout her experience, producing 21 paintings and a short diary that began as private acts of processing and calm. They were first shared at The Peripheral Space in November 2025, an event where the idea for the book was born.

Uninvited gathers the work into an illustrated collection exploring fear, vulnerability, hope, resilience and gratitude. Erica Smith, who worked with Helen on the design of the book, calls it 'a remarkable combination of words and her paintings'.

title: Council's free business support pilot to visit Hastings Old Town and Rye high streets
text:
A new free business support pilot will reach independent shops and businesses in selected East Sussex high streets, including Hastings Old Town and Rye, the county council said.

According to an East Sussex County Council spokesperson, the pilot brings free, practical one-to-one support directly to independent businesses in Rye, Seaford, Newhaven, Mayfield, Eastbourne Old Town and Hastings Old Town. Businesses can receive tailored advice and a clear action plan focused on their own priorities, with support on topics including sales, customer loyalty, marketing, pricing, profitability and making better use of retail space.

The outreach team will visit businesses directly, the council said. The programme is funded by HM Government, East Sussex County Council and the East Sussex Growth Hub, and is managed by the county council and delivered by Smarter Society.

title: On this day 1944: Hastings' secret evacuation plans revealed
text:
On Saturday 21 October 1944, the Hastings and St Leonards Observer printed what the town had not been allowed to know during the war: the full story of the secret plans to evacuate the whole borough in the event of a German invasion.

Complete plans had been prepared for the compulsory evacuation of everyone still in Hastings after the voluntary schemes, with only about a thousand people, Home Guard, civil defence and essential services staff, required to stay behind. The scheme ran in stages: school-age children first, then the remaining civilians, and a joint plan for a grave and immediate emergency.

The Observer described how the Southern Railway worked out a secret timetable of special trains from all five stations between Ore and West Marina, each to carry 800 people, with the entire movement to be finished in three days. Extra luggage had to be packed and left at set points in town for forwarding to reception areas in Kent and Surrey, because evacuees could take only light hand luggage, and a circular went to every mother in September 1941 listing what her child would need to bring.

The plans were kept under revision until late in the war; the Regional Commissioner's direction was only cancelled at the end of September 1944. Hastings was spared the need for them, but the Observer noted the town's civilian preparations would have stood the test and 'a vital factor in the defence of Britain'.
